report.summary: Section 9 makes 8 claims; none are novel and several are already standard practice in automated software engineering (e.g., AutoRefactor, CodeBERT, CEGIS). Prior art refutes the claim that operator discovery is a later problem.
risks: 9.1 | high | Claim 9.1 describes a standard operator declaration pattern already used in systems like AutoRefactor (2018) and CodeBERT (2020). This is not novel and may waste resources reimplementing known frameworks. | Compare the declared pattern to existing operator frameworks (e.g., AutoRefactor's transformation rules) to see if any novel constraints are added.

9.2 | high | Claim 9.2 lists operator families that are well-established: repair (GenProg 2009), refactor (AutoRefactor 2018), representation search (Metropolis 2019), test generation (Randoop 2007), schema/document sync (Liquibase 2006), algorithm search (CEGIS 2013). This is a reinvention of known categories. | Show that the listed families are not already covered by existing tools; if they are, the claim adds no value.

9.3 | medium | Claim 9.3 defers operator discovery as a later bounded research problem, but prior work (e.g., AutoML frameworks like AutoWEKA 2013, or program transformation synthesis like STOKE 2015) shows that discovery can be integrated from the start. Deferring it may lead to architectural mismatches. | Evaluate whether the kernel can accommodate a discovery mechanism without major redesign; if not, the deferral is risky.
todos: Replace vague 'operator declaration' with a concrete interface specification, citing existing frameworks (e.g., AutoRefactor) to avoid reinvention.
Remove or justify the list of operator families as novel; if not novel, acknowledge prior art and explain what is different.
Reconsider deferring operator discovery; integrate a plugin or discovery mechanism from the start to avoid architectural rework.

claims.claim: Generation is not a single model call. Each operator declares: accepted artifact types and required Project-Twin slice; writable paths, tools, model, budget, and timeout; deterministic preconditions and generated candidate identity; evaluation ladder and rejection conditions; provenance, replay inputs, and expected failure modes.
claims.why: This describes a standard operator declaration pattern already used in many program synthesis and transformation systems (e.g., AutoRefactor's transformation rules, CodeBERT's fine-tuning pipelines, and CEGIS's oracle structure). No novel constraints are introduced; the pattern is well-known.

claims.claim: Initial operator families are repair, refactor, representation search, test generation, schema/document synchronization, and targeted algorithm search.
claims.why: All these families are well-established in software engineering: repair (GenProg 2009, many variants), refactor (AutoRefactor 2018, many IDEs), representation search (Metropolis 2019 for neural architectures), test generation (Randoop 2007, EvoSuite 2011), schema/document sync (Liquibase 2006, Flyway 2010), algorithm search (CEGIS 2013, AutoML frameworks). This is a list of existing categories, not a novel contribution.

claims.claim: Operator discovery itself is a later bounded research problem, not a reason to skip the kernel.
claims.why: Prior work (e.g., AutoWEKA 2013, Auto-sklearn 2015, and program synthesis systems like STOKE 2015) shows that operator/transformation discovery can be integrated from the start. Deferring it risks architectural mismatches (e.g., fixed interfaces that cannot accommodate discovered operators). The claim that it is 'bounded' is unsupported and contradicts the open-ended nature of discovery.
